## Web Development Company in Pune: What AI Browser Agents Mean for Your Website in 2026

If you've checked your server logs recently and noticed traffic that behaves like a human — clicking buttons, filling forms, scrolling in bursts — but never triggers a mouse-move event or lingers on a page the way a person does, you're not imagining it. Agentic browsers that click, type and check out on a person's behalf are now a real, measurable share of traffic to Indian business websites, and a web development company in Pune building sites in 2026 needs a plan for them that goes beyond the usual bot-blocking reflex.

This isn't the same conversation as "AI crawlers and llms.txt" that dominated 2025. Crawlers like GPTBot or ClaudeBot fetch your pages once, in bulk, to train models or answer questions later — they never click a button on your site. Agentic browsers are different: a real person opens ChatGPT, Perplexity, or Chrome, asks it to "book a slot with this clinic" or "buy this from that store," and the AI drives an actual browser session — logging in, filling forms, clicking "Pay Now" — on a live page your site is currently serving. That is a fundamentally different technical problem from content ingestion, and most business websites in Pune were never built with it in mind.

### The three agentic browsers you're actually seeing traffic from

As of September 2026, three products account for almost all agentic browsing traffic reaching Indian websites:

- **Perplexity Comet** — Perplexity's own agentic browser, now free worldwide and running on Android, making it the most accessible option for Indian users on modest data plans and a common source of agent-driven sessions on price-comparison and local-business searches.
- **Google's Gemini in Chrome** — Google folded a Gemini agent directly into Chrome, the browser already installed on more than 3 billion devices, which means agentic capability reached the largest possible base overnight rather than requiring anyone to download a new app.
- **ChatGPT Atlas** — OpenAI's standalone agentic browser, launched October 2025, was discontinued as a standalone product on 9 August 2026, less than ten months after launch, and will not receive further security patches. If your analytics still show an "Atlas" user agent, that traffic is coming from a browser its own maker has stopped maintaining — worth flagging to your security team, not just your marketing one.

The practical detail that catches most developers off guard: Atlas and Comet are both built on the Chromium engine. Run a basic user-agent or fingerprint check and an agentic session can look almost identical to a person using ordinary Chrome. Bot-detection rules tuned to catch "obviously automated" traffic (headless browsers, missing JS execution, no cookies) routinely wave these sessions straight through — or, just as often, misfire and block a genuine customer who happens to be using one of these tools to reach you.

### How an agentic session is actually different from a crawler hit

It helps to be precise about what's happening at the request level, because the fix depends on it. A crawler visit is stateless: one request, no login, no session cookie, no intent to complete a transaction. An agentic browsing session is the opposite on every count — it authenticates with real (or agent-managed) credentials, carries session cookies exactly as a logged-in customer would, executes your site's JavaScript, and works through a multi-step flow the way a human would with a keyboard and a lot of patience. From your server's point of view, distinguishing the two isn't a robots.txt decision; it's a session-behaviour decision, which is why the two problems need separate rules rather than one blanket "block AI traffic" toggle.

This distinction matters most on the pages a crawler would never touch anyway: login screens, multi-step forms, appointment calendars, and checkout. A content page rendering slightly oddly for a crawler is a minor SEO nuisance. A checkout flow that an agentic browser can't complete on behalf of a paying customer is a lost sale, in real time, that your analytics will likely misreport as an abandoned cart rather than a technical failure.

### Why "just block bots" stops working here

Most WordPress and custom-built sites in Pune lean on a security plugin or a WAF rule that blocks anything that "looks automated." That approach made sense when the automated traffic hitting your site was almost entirely scrapers and spam bots with nothing to gain from behaving politely. It breaks down with agentic browsers for two reasons.

First, the session is initiated by an actual customer with actual intent to transact — blocking it outright is lost revenue, not blocked abuse. Second, over-aggressive CAPTCHA and bot-challenge pages are exactly where these agents currently fail. Reporting on agentic browsers through 2026 has repeatedly flagged CAPTCHAs, multi-step OTP flows and JavaScript-heavy interactive widgets as the most common points where an agent-driven checkout simply stalls, leaving a frustrated (real) customer stuck mid-purchase with no clear way to intervene. If your [website's checkout or booking flow](/services/checkout-system) puts a CAPTCHA in front of every transaction regardless of risk signal, you're not stopping bad actors — you're stopping a growing share of your actual customers.

### What to actually build for

None of this means throwing out your existing security posture. It means moving from "block anything automated" to "identify what the session is trying to do, and let legitimate intent through."

**1. Keep forms and checkouts usable without a mouse.** Agentic browsers interact with the DOM more like assistive technology than like a human clicking pixels — they look for labelled form fields, accessible button text, and a predictable tab order. A form built with vague `<div onclick>` elements instead of real `<button>` and `<label>` tags was already a problem for screen-reader users; now it's also a problem for the growing share of your traffic arriving through an AI agent. This is the same semantic-HTML discipline accessibility audits have asked for all along, and it happens to be exactly what makes a page usable by an agent too.

**2. Risk-tier your CAPTCHA and OTP challenges, don't blanket them.** Reserve hard challenges for the actual risk signals that matter — new device plus high-value transaction plus mismatched billing details — rather than firing a CAPTCHA on every single checkout. A tiered approach keeps friction where it earns its keep (fraud prevention) without stalling every agent-assisted purchase, which is now a routine and legitimate way real customers shop.

**3. Separate "agent reading your content" from "agent acting on your site" in your logging.** Your `robots.txt` and crawler rules for GPTBot, ClaudeBot and PerplexityBot are a content-ingestion decision — a separate policy question from what happens when an agentic browser, on behalf of a logged-in or checking-out customer, hits your `/checkout` or `/book-appointment` endpoint. Conflating the two in one WAF rule is how sites end up either blocking real customers or leaving checkout completely unguarded. Log user-agent strings and request patterns separately for the two cases so you can actually tell them apart when something goes wrong.

**4. Watch for stale, unmaintained agents in your traffic.** ChatGPT Atlas's shutdown is the clearest example so far of a pattern likely to repeat as this category matures fast: an agentic browser with real installed base can be discontinued with no further security patches, while some fraction of users keep running it anyway. Treat unmaintained agent user-agents as a slightly elevated risk category in your fraud rules, the same way you would an outdated mobile app version that stopped receiving updates.

**5. Test your own critical flows with an agent before a customer's does.** Rather than guessing where an agentic session might fail, run your own booking form, quote request, or checkout through Gemini in Chrome or Perplexity Comet as a test. It takes under an hour and reliably surfaces the same handful of issues: an unlabelled dropdown, a date picker that only responds to a specific click sequence, or a "confirm" step hidden behind a hover state. Fixing those also improves the experience for every human visitor using a keyboard, a screen reader, or a slow connection.

### Payment gateways and fraud rules need the same conversation

If your site takes payments directly rather than through a marketplace, the agentic-browser question doesn't stop at the checkout form — it extends into how your [payment gateway integration](/services/payment-gateway) scores risk. Most Indian gateways build fraud rules around signals like device fingerprint consistency, typing cadence, and time-on-page before submission, because those signals reliably separated humans from bots for the better part of a decade. An agentic browser breaks several of those assumptions at once: it can fill a multi-field form in under a second, it doesn't move a mouse the way a human does, and it may be running on a device fingerprint the gateway hasn't seen paired with that card before.

None of this means an agent-driven purchase is automatically fraudulent — plenty of it is a real customer buying a real product faster than they could type it themselves. But it does mean a fraud-scoring model tuned only on pre-2026 behaviour will flag a rising share of legitimate transactions as suspicious, generating false declines that look, from the merchant's side, like inexplicably dropping conversion rates on certain days or certain product categories. If your gateway allows custom risk rules, it's worth asking your provider directly whether their model has been retrained to account for agentic traffic, rather than assuming it has.

### Measuring the shift instead of guessing at it

Most Indian business owners asking about this want a number, and the honest answer is that a single industry-wide figure doesn't exist yet — adoption is moving too fast, and it varies too much by sector, for any one statistic to stay accurate for long. What's more useful is building the measurement into your own analytics so you can track your own trend rather than relying on someone else's headline number.

This is a narrower, session-behaviour question than the "AI referral traffic" tracking most digital marketing teams have started adding to GA4 over the past year, which mainly measures how many visitors arrive after being pointed to your site by a chatbot's answer. What you're measuring here is different: not where the visit came from, but whether the visit itself is being driven by an agent once it lands on your site. A practical, low-effort version of this is a custom GA4 dimension that captures the user-agent string on key conversion events — form submission, checkout start, checkout complete — filtered for the known Comet, Gemini-agent and (legacy) Atlas signatures. Over a quarter or two, that gives you an actual trend line specific to your own traffic and your own conversion funnel, rather than a number lifted from a global report that may not reflect an Indian audience in your category at all.

It's also worth checking that trend line against your abandoned-cart and form-drop-off reports specifically. If agent-driven sessions are climbing while your abandonment rate at a particular step is climbing in parallel, that step is very likely the one an agent is struggling to complete — which turns an abstract "AI trend" into a concrete, fixable item on your development backlog.

### A short, practical checklist

- Audit form fields for real `<label>` associations, not placeholder text standing in for a label
- Confirm every actionable element is a real `<button>` or `<a>`, not a styled `<div>` with a click handler
- Map where CAPTCHA and OTP challenges fire, and whether they're tied to a risk score or applied indiscriminately
- Separate your crawler-access policy (robots.txt, llms.txt) from your live-session bot-management rules
- Run one full checkout or booking flow through an agentic browser yourself, quarterly, as a regression test
- Log agent user-agent strings separately from generic "bot" traffic so you can see the split over time

### Frequently asked questions

**How much of my traffic is actually agentic browsers right now?**
For most Indian small-business sites it's still a small minority of sessions, and the honest answer is that the exact share varies enormously by category — travel booking, ticketing and e-commerce sites report noticeably more agent-driven sessions than, say, a local clinic's appointment page. Rather than chasing a precise percentage, the more useful exercise is checking your own logs for Comet, Atlas and Gemini-agent user-agent strings over a month and seeing whether the number is trending up.

**Do I need a different version of my site for AI agents?**
No. Everything described above is a refinement of the same site you already have — better semantic markup, smarter CAPTCHA placement, cleaner form structure — not a parallel "AI-only" build. Vendors selling a separate "agent-ready" website product are, in most cases, selling you the accessibility and UX audit you should be doing anyway.

**Does this affect WordPress sites differently from custom-built ones?**
Not fundamentally, but the failure points differ. WordPress sites built with heavy page-builder plugins are more likely to render interactive elements as non-semantic `<div>` structures that both screen readers and agentic browsers struggle with, while custom-built React or Vue sites are more likely to hide state changes behind client-side JavaScript that an agent's DOM reader has to wait for. Either way, the diagnostic — test your key flows with an agent, then fix what breaks — is the same.

**What does this cost to fix?**
For most sites this is an audit, not a rebuild: a half-day to a full-day review of your forms, checkout, and CAPTCHA configuration, followed by targeted markup and configuration fixes rather than a platform change. Where it does become a larger job is on older sites built entirely with non-semantic markup, where the fix genuinely does touch most templates on the site — in those cases it's worth folding into a broader [website redesign](/services/website-creation) rather than patching page by page.

**Should I block agentic browsers entirely until this settles down?**
We'd advise against it for any site that sells something or captures leads. Blocking a Chromium-based agentic session outright, given how closely it resembles ordinary Chrome traffic, tends to require rules broad enough that they also catch a meaningful share of genuine human visitors on the same browser. The lower-risk path is the one this article has laid out: fix the underlying markup and risk-tiering issues that make agent sessions fail, which also happens to fix real accessibility and conversion problems that were already costing you customers.

### Where a web development company in Pune should start

If you're not sure whether your site's checkout or lead-capture forms would survive an agentic browser session cleanly, that's a short technical audit, not a rebuild: check your form markup for real labels and button elements, review where CAPTCHA fires and whether it's tied to risk signals, and separate your crawler-access rules from your live-session security rules. As a [web development company in Pune](/services/website-creation), we build this into every new site we deliver and can audit an existing one against it — [get in touch with our team](/contact-us) to have your checkout and booking flows reviewed against agentic-browser behaviour before it becomes a support ticket.

Govindani Infotech builds and maintains business websites, e-commerce stores and NGO donation platforms across Pune and pan-India, and this kind of behavioural audit — testing real flows the way a customer's tools now actually use them — has become a standard part of how we review a site before and after launch.
